title: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning and Data
text: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning and Data
Computer systems designed to perform tasks that commonly require human-like capabilities: recognizing  patterns, understanding language, classifying               information or interpreting images.
An approach within AI in which systems learn patterns from data rather than relying exclusively on explicitly programmed rules.
For many machine-learning applications, examples of data and their correct labels are used to train or.         evaluate models. Those labels come from annotation work.
Annotation is not a side activity. For supervised learning the labeled dataset is the teaching material the model learns from, which is why annotation quality sets a ceiling on model quality.
Keep this section short and concrete. Trainees do not need machine-learning theory; they need to understand why their      labels matter and what happens downstream if they are wrong.
notes:
Three definitions, kept deliberately brief. Avoid going deeper into model architectures — it is not needed and it loses non-technical trainees.
Useful framing: the model does not know anything about cars. It only knows what thousands of people told it a car looks like. If those people disagreed, the model learns the disagreement.
Ask for a show of hands: who has used a product that relies on this (voice assistants, photo search, translation)? Connect the abstract to something they use.

title: What Is Data lbeling?
text: Assigning meaningful labels, categories, annotations or other structured information to raw data so it can be used for AI development, evaluation or related analysis.
Identify whether an image contains a vehicle
Draw a bounding box around each vehicle
Convert spoken words into written text
Identify a speaker, sound event or noise category where required
Classify a message into an agreed category
Identify and track specified objects across frames
THE RULE THAT GOVERNS EVERY TASK
The correct annotation depends on the task specification. A label that is appropriate for one project may be incorrect for    another  so there is no such thing as a universally "right" label.
notes:
Work down the table and ask participants which of these they expect to encounter on their projects.
The callout is the single most important sentence in this module. Say it twice. Trainees frequently carry rules from one project into another and create inconsistency that is expensive to fix.
Anticipated question: 'What if I think the guideline is wrong?' Answer: you record it as a clarification request and escalate it; you do not quietly apply your own interpretation. This is covered fully on Day 2.

title: Why Data Quality Matters
text: Poor-quality annotations introduce errors into training data and undermine the reliability of downstream AI systems.
Fatigue, rushed work or poorly managed workloads.

A model trained on inconsistent labels learns the inconsistency. Volume does not compensate for error: a large dataset                   annotated badly is less useful than a small dataset annotated correctly and consistently.
Ensure learners understand both the procedure and the reasoning behind the annotation rules. A trainee who knows only the rule cannot handle a case the rule does not cover.
notes:
Run the GIGO point as a short discussion rather than a statement. Ask: if you had to choose between 10,000 images labelled by untrained people and 1,000 labelled by a calibrated team, which would you take, and why?
Note that most causes in the left-hand card are management failures, not annotator failures. That matters for tomorrow: blaming annotators for a guideline problem does not fix anything.
Second callout is the core trainer message of Day 1: teach the reason, not just the rule.

title: When Two Annotators Disagree
text: A project requires annotators to identify cars in images. One annotator labels only passenger cars. Another labels cars, buses       and trucks under the same category. Both complete their tasks quickly, but the results are inconsistent because they interpreted   the category differently.
THE CORRECT RESPONSE  —  FIVE STEPS, IN ORDER
Review the guideline.  Establish what the approved specification actually says about the category.
Clarify the category definition.  Resolve the ambiguity with the authorized project or client contact.
Provide examples.  Show positive and negative cases, including the edge cases that caused the split.
Conduct a calibration exercise.  Have both annotators re-label the same samples and compare.
Assess completed work.  Decide whether previously completed work needs correction, and how much.
notes:
This example recurs throughout the programme — use it as the standard reference case.
Key teaching point: neither annotator was lazy and neither was careless. Both worked fast and both followed what they believed the instruction said. The failure is in the specification and in the absence of calibration.
Ask the room what most teams do instead (tell the annotators to be more careful) and why that fails — because it leaves the ambiguity in place and the same split recurs next week.
Step 5 is the one people forget. Work already submitted under the wrong interpretation does not correct itself.

title: Questions for the Group
text: Work in pairs for five minutes, then report back. There is no single correct wording — look for reasoning.
How would you explain AI to a 10-year-old?Do you think AI is making life easier or more complicated?
Why is data important in AI development?What is the difference between classifying an image and.  identifying objects within it?
Why must annotators follow the same approved                 guidelines?
Can you name one AI tool you have heard of?
notes:
Expected answers, for your own reference:
1. Size does not guarantee quality. Inconsistent, incorrect or unrepresentative labels teach the model the wrong pattern regardless of volume.
2. Classification assigns a label to the whole image ('this image contains a vehicle'). Object detection locates and bounds each instance within the image.
3. Because consistency is what makes the dataset usable. Individually reasonable but differing interpretations produce contradictory training signals.
4. Record it as a clarification request, escalate to the authorised contact, wait for a decision, then communicate the approved interpretation to everyone — not just the person who asked. Do not invent a rule.
Note for participants: question 4 is exactly what they will be assessed on when they teach.

title: The AI Solution Development Lifecycle
text: Six stages from problem to deployment. Data labeling is stage three, and the quality of its output sets the ceiling for every stage after it.
Agree what the system must do, who it  is for and what success looks like.
Gather representative data of the right  type, volume and quality.
Apply the approved specification to       produce accurate, consistent labels.
The model learns patterns from the         labeled examples it is given.
Measure performance against held-out data and the agreed acceptance criteria.
Release, monitor in use, and feed findings back into the cycle.
Stages four to six can only be as good as the labelled data they inherit. Inconsistent labels do not average out with volume ; they are learned, measured as success, and deployed.
notes:
Use this as the orientation slide for where annotation work sits.
Walk the cycle once, briefly, then stop at stage three. The point of the slide is not the six boxes; it is that everything downstream inherits whatever stage three produces.
Ask the group what happens at stage five if stage three was inconsistent. The answer people miss: the model is validated against test data labelled by the same team, with the same misunderstanding, so it passes validation and fails in use.
Note the loop back from stage six. Deployment is not the end — findings in use generate new data requirements, guideline changes and further labeling, which is why guideline version control and effective dates matter.

title: Nine Stages, From Intake to Close-Out
text: Nine Stages, From Intake to Close-Out
Confirm task, data, volume, deadline and requirements
PM, QA lead and client contact

The sequence may be adapted to the project, but readiness, quality control and accountability must not be omitted.

Make clear the 'Responsibility' column is illustrative; actual accountability follows the agreed project structure.

title: Semantic Segmentation
text: Every pixel in the image is given a class label, turning the whole scene into a colour-coded map.
Fill each region with its class colour
Keep borders tight where classes meet
notes: Semantic segmentation labels every pixel. Point out that each colour is a class, not an individual object: all cars share one colour. Emphasise that no pixel may be left unlabelled.

title: Polyline
text: Connected line segments trace thin, continuous structures that have length but no real area.
Place points along the line, end to end
Add more points wherever the line curves
Keep each line one continuous object
Example: both road edges and the centre line traced point by point
notes: Polylines are for things that are long and thin, such as lane markings, kerbs, cables and rivers. The annotator clicks points along the line; more points are needed on curves.

title: Polygon
text: Points placed around an object’s edge form a closed shape that follows its exact outline.
Click vertices along the object’s edge
Add points wherever the outline bends
Close the shape back at the first point
Example: a person, a car and a tree outlined vertex by vertex
notes: Polygons give a much tighter fit than a box, which matters for irregular shapes like people and trees. Compare the tree outline here with the bounding box on the next slide.

title: Bounding Box
text: A rectangle drawn tightly around each object shows where it is and what it is.
Draw one box per object, then label it
Flag objects that are hidden or cut off
Example: three cars, a person and a traffic light, each in its own box
notes: Bounding boxes are the fastest and most common technique. The key quality rule is tightness: the box touches the object’s edges with no gap and nothing cut off. Even small, distant cars get their own box.

title: Key Point
text: Single points mark specific landmarks, such as body joints, so shape and movement can be measured.
Place each point on its exact landmark
Follow the point order in the guideline
Example: 17 body keypoints joined into a skeleton
notes: Key points are about precise position and consistent order: left shoulder is always point 6, for example. When a joint is hidden, annotators still mark it but flag it as occluded, as the guideline specifies.

title: LiDAR and Big Data
text: Two further areas. One is annotation in three dimensions; the other is the data engineering that surrounds every annotation project.
Annotation of three-dimensional point-cloud data, where depth and orientation matter.
Label every point in a scan according to its approved class.
Enclose objects in three dimensions, with position and orientation.
The engineering around the labeling: where data comes from, how it is prepared, stored, reported and built on.
Database   Structure, store and maintain project datasets.
Data Visualization   Turn production and quality data into readable reporting.
Data Crawling   Collect source data at scale from agreed origins.
Data Preparation   Clean, format and organise raw data before annotation.
Software Development   Build the tooling and integrations the work depends on.

LiDAR is annotation work with its own tools and acceptance criteria. Big Data is what makes any annotation project possible — without prepared data and reliable reporting, the labeling cannot start or be measured.
notes:
Two areas with very different character, which is why they are presented differently.
LiDAR is annotation in three dimensions. It needs suitable data, suitable tools and more practice than the 2D techniques — navigating a point cloud is the hardest part for new annotators, not the labeling rule.
Big Data is not annotation at all. It is the surrounding engineering: where the data comes from, how it is cleaned and stored, and how production and quality figures are reported back. Annotators rarely see it, but every delay in data preparation shows up later as idle annotation capacity.
If asked how these relate to the training: LiDAR techniques appear in the annotation week as 3D bounding box and 3D semantic segmentation; Big Data does not, and is a separate service line.

title: 3D Segmentation
text: Every point in a LiDAR scan is labelled with its class, so the       whole 3D scene is understood.
Label every point with its approved class
Rotate the scan to check from all angles
Keep clean edges where classes touch
notes: A LiDAR scan is a cloud of 3D points measured by laser. 3D segmentation gives every point a class, the 3D version of semantic segmentation. Point out the rings on the ground (each is one laser beam) and the dark gaps behind cars and people, where the laser cannot see.

title: 3D Bounding Box
text: A 3D box (cuboid) encloses each object, recording its position, size and the direction it faces.
Fit length, width and height to the points
Turn the box to face the direction of travel
Keep box sizes steady across frames
Example: points coloured by height; the white line on each box shows which way the object faces
notes: Unlike a 2D box, a cuboid has depth and a heading. The white line on top of each box shows which way the object faces; the oncoming car’s box points the other way. Boxes should hug the points and keep the same size for the same object across frames.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR AN ANNOTATOR
You will rarely be told which product your labels end up in. Treat every task as if the output were going into use tomorrow, because in most of these sectors it is.
notes:
The two original slides have been combined. Splitting ten sectors across two identical layouts made the list look like two different things when it is one.
Do not read the list. Pick three sectors the group will recognise and describe what the annotation work actually looks like in each — the right-hand column gives you the line for every one.
Useful question for the room: which of these sectors would be most affected by a labeling error, and why? Healthcare, automobile and defense usually come up, which opens the point about critical criteria that cannot be compensated for by a good overall score.
The callout is the behavioural point. Annotators who assume their work is a training exercise treat it differently from those who assume it is going into production.

Procurement reform, civil-servant training, government use cases, and GhanaChat.
Pillars 1 and 2 build people. Pillars 3 to 5 build the conditions. Pillars 6 to 8 put AI to work and the state is last, holding itself to the same standard it asks of industry.
notes:
Do not read all eight. Group them: people (1–2), conditions (3–5), application (6–8).
Pillar 3 contains the line most relevant to annotation work ; local-language datasets  and pillar 7 names an NLP Centre of Excellence and the digitalisation of oral histories. Both are language-data commitments that need people who can collect, transcribe and label Ghanaian languages.
Pillar 8 and GhanaChat usually draw the most interest in a room. It is worth asking what training data a Ghana-specific government language model would need, and who would produce it.
Pillar 4 is the governance counterweight: open data and sharing agreements on one side, data protection and privacy on the other. Link it to Act 843 obligations the audience already works under.

title: KENYA AI STRATEGY 2025–2030
text: Kenya’s national strategy to become Africa’s hub for AI research, innovation and commercialization ethical, inclusive, secure and locally relevant.
To become a regional leader in AI research, development, innovation and commercialisation for inclusive socioeconomic development.
Use local talent, data and innovation to improve economic growth and public services across priority sectors.
Local-first. AI designed in Kenya, trained on Kenyan data and serving Kenyan languages and contexts  rather than imported wholesale and adapted afterwards.
notes:
Open with the vision statement and let it sit for a moment. The phrase that matters is 'research, development, innovation and commercialisation’ ; Kenya is not positioning itself as a consumer market for AI but as a place where AI is built and sold.
The seven guiding principles are not decoration. Several of them 1. inclusion, cultural relevance and a local-first approach 2. translate directly into demand for locally produced, locally understood training data, which is the work this audience does.
The Kenyan flag colours are used deliberately on the vision band; keep that restraint if you adapt the deck.
Good framing question: what does 'locally relevant' mean in practice for a model that has to work in Kiswahili, Sheng and several regional languages?

title: Three Pillars, Four Enablers
text: The strategy rests on three delivery pillars, supported by four cross-cutting enablers that make the pillars usable, safe, funded and fair.
High-performance computing; three AI-       capable data centres in five years.
Stronger cybersecurity, powered by green  energy.
Data governance, secure sharing and interoperability standards.
High-quality local datasets for training AI models.
Funding for localised models and startup  scaling.
Markets created for Kenyan AI products.
AI foundations in schools, specialised tertiary and industry training, placements and apprenticeships.
National AI policy, risk and safety standards, regulatory sandboxes, and AI-specific legislation in time.
Grants, funds, public-private partnerships, special economic zones and investment incentives.
Ethical impact assessments, complaint and redress mechanisms, bias and representation, public AI literacy.
The pillars build capability. The enablers decide whether that capability is trusted, affordable, staffed and fairly distributed — which is why all four run across all three.
notes:
The structure is the message: three pillars that build capability, four enablers that determine whether it is usable.
Pillar 2 is the one closest to this audience. 'High-quality local datasets for training AI models' is a policy commitment to exactly the work annotators and QA reviewers do, and it is the line to point at when someone asks whether annotation is a long-term career.
Pillar 1 carries the only hard, dated commitment on the slide: three AI-capable data centres within five years. Expect that to be the number people remember.
Enabler 7 pairs with the training's ethics content: ethical impact assessments in public-sector AI and citizen redress mechanisms are the governance equivalent of the quality-assurance discipline taught here.

title: Strengths, Gaps and Risks
text: An honest reading of the starting position, and the first applications the strategy intends to deliver.
Mobile and fibre infrastructure, plus data  centres.
Government support; growing AI use in.    key sectors.
Limited computing capacity and uneven   access.
Low public trust; underfunded local research and startups.
Wider urban–rural and social digital divide.
Dependence on foreign infrastructure and technology.
Intelligent tutoring and multilingual teacher tools
AI platform for the creative industries
Not only an AI user, but a producer of trusted, locally designed AI solutions.
notes:
The strengths and gaps columns should be read against each other: Kenya has the energy, the connectivity and the entrepreneurs, and lacks the skills, the data and the computing capacity. Two of those three gaps are addressable by training and by annotation work.
'Insufficient quality and digitised data' is the gap this audience closes. Say so directly.
On risks, resist treating the list as a disclaimer. Job displacement and the urban–rural divide are live concerns for trainees, and the honest answer is that the strategy creates one kind of work while automating another — which is the argument for moving up from annotation into QA, project management and training.
The five priority applications are all language- and context-dependent, which is the practical case for local data and local annotators. Close on the dark band.

title: Why Africa’s Participation in AI Matters
text: Why Africa’s Participation in AI Matters
The same six reasons, laid out without the map — use this version where the slide has to carry the argument on its own.
Africa’s languages, cultures and contexts    reduce global AI bias and improve model    accuracy for everyone.
Home to more than 1.4 billion people and    the world’s youngest, fastest-growing        population.
AI built in Africa addresses challenges in     healthcare, agriculture, climate adaptation, financial inclusion and education.
High-value digital jobs, startups and exportable tech services that accelerate economic growth.
African voices ensure global AI rules reflect developing-world realities, not only Global North priorities.
Resource-efficient solutions drive frugal,    scalable AI innovations that are valuable    worldwide.
Without Africa, AI risks being biased, incomplete and globally ineffective.
notes:
Alternative to the previous slide, without the map. Keep one and delete the other ;do not present both.
Use this version when the slide has to stand on its own, for example in a printed pack or when it is sent ahead of a session without a facilitator to talk over it.
Use the map version when you are presenting live and want something to point at while you make the data-diversity argument.
The content is identical, so the speaker notes for the previous slide apply here as well.

notes: Project reporting is treated in the ToT on Day 2: the daily report, production tracker, issue log and progress report, built from SYNAPSE project data. On the right, SYNAPSE sits at the centre because once you know it, the other tools feel familiar. Image editors and design tools use the same zoom, layers, selection and shape logic as the labeling canvas. ArcGIS works with polygons on map layers, just like polygon labeling. Excel, PowerPoint and Word turn SYNAPSE exports into reports. Knowing how training data is made helps you use Generative AI well. And other labeling platforms such as CVAT or Label Studio run the same tasks and QA with a different interface. Photoshop, Figma, Canva, ArcGIS and other labeling platforms are suggested next steps rather than part of the programme.
